```{r}
source("R/helpers.R")
set.seed(STUDENT_SEED)

make_result <- function(name,
                        generator,
                        theoretical_mean,
                        theoretical_sd,
                        decision_text) {
  means <- simulate_sample_means(generator)
  summary <- summarize_sample_means(
    means,
    theoretical_mean = theoretical_mean,
    theoretical_sd = theoretical_sd
  )

  first_screened <- summary$sample_size[summary$screening_rule][1]
  if (length(first_screened) == 0 || is.na(first_screened)) {
    first_screened <- NA_real_
  }

  selected_row <- summary[summary$sample_size == first_screened, , drop = FALSE]

  data.frame(
    population = name,
    first_screening_n = first_screened,
    simulated_mean_at_first = ifelse(
      is.na(first_screened), NA,
      summary$simulated_mean[summary$sample_size == first_screened]
    ),
    simulated_sd_at_first = ifelse(
      is.na(first_screened), NA,
      summary$simulated_sd[summary$sample_size == first_screened]
    ),
    theoretical_se_at_first = ifelse(
      is.na(first_screened), NA,
      summary$theoretical_se[summary$sample_size == first_screened]
    ),
    skewness_at_first = ifelse(
      is.na(first_screened), NA,
      selected_row$skewness
    ),
    excess_kurtosis_at_first = ifelse(
      is.na(first_screened), NA,
      selected_row$excess_kurtosis
    ),
    decision = decision_text,
    row.names = NULL
  )
}

normal_results <- make_result(
  "Standard Normal",
  function(n) rnorm(n, 0, 1),
  0,
  1,
  "Normal from the start"
)

die_results <- make_result(
  "Six-sided die",
  function(n) sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE),
  3.5,
  sqrt(35 / 12),
  "Discrete, then smoother"
)

exponential_results <- make_result(
  "Exponential",
  function(n) rexp(n, rate = 1),
  1,
  1,
  "Right skew needed larger n"
)

binomial_results <- make_result(
  "Small Binomial",
  function(n) rbinom(n, size = 5, prob = 0.10),
  0.5,
  sqrt(5 * 0.10 * 0.90),
  "Skew and discreteness slowed it"
)

screening_summary <- rbind(
  normal_results,
  die_results,
  exponential_results,
  binomial_results,
  data.frame(
    population = "Cauchy",
    first_screening_n = NA_real_,
    simulated_mean_at_first = NA_real_,
    simulated_sd_at_first = NA_real_,
    theoretical_se_at_first = NA_real_,
    skewness_at_first = NA_real_,
    excess_kurtosis_at_first = NA_real_,
    decision = "Ordinary CLT not applicable",
    row.names = NULL
  )
)
```

## What I investigated

For each population, I repeatedly generated samples, calculated their means,
and studied the distribution of those means. The number of observations in one
sample is `n`; the number of repeated samples is 10,000. These are different
quantities.

I used the same basic rule for the four finite-variance populations. I looked
for a roughly bell-shaped histogram, a fairly straight Q-Q plot, skewness close
to zero, and excess kurtosis close to zero. I also checked whether the
simulated standard error was close to the theoretical value. As a numerical
starting point, I used absolute skewness no larger than 0.15 and absolute
excess kurtosis no larger than 0.30. I used the graphs as well, instead of
trusting the two cutoffs alone.

## Comparison table

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  print_summary(screening_summary),
  caption = "Initial numerical screening; standard-error fields are not applicable to Cauchy"
)
```

The `first_screening_n` column is only a starting point. The final written
conclusion also considers the plots. The skewness and kurtosis columns show the
diagnostics at the first screened sample size. The Cauchy population is shown
with `NA` because its usual mean and variance do not exist.

## Main findings

### Standard Normal

The population is already normal, so its sample means are normal for every
sample size under the model. Increasing `n` reduces the standard error but does
not need to create normality from a non-normal starting population.

### Six-sided die

The original population is discrete and uniform. Its sample means become less
visibly discrete as `n` increases, and the CLT gives an approximately normal
shape after enough observations. The simulated standard error can be compared
directly with `sqrt(35 / 12) / sqrt(n)`.

### Exponential

The Exponential population begins strongly right-skewed. Its sample means
usually need more observations before the skewness is small and the Q-Q plot is
reasonably linear. This shows why the shortcut `n = 30` is not a universal rule.

### Small Binomial

The Small Binomial population is both discrete and right-skewed. Its means can
take many more possible values as `n` increases, which helps the sampling
distribution look smoother. Its results should be judged with both numerical
and graphical evidence.

### Cauchy

The Cauchy situation is different from the other four cases. It is characterized
by no regular mean and variance, thus the regular CLT assumptions and formulae
for the standard error do not apply. Even if `n` is large, it is possible that
extreme observations continue to dominate the given sample means. Therefore, the
statement “under no sample size is it possible to apply the ordinary CLT” is a
justifiable conclusion.

## Is `n = 30` a rule that is always correct?

No. The outcome of the experiments demonstrates that the answer depends on the
population. Thus, normal population results in quick good behavior of the CLT,
symmetric discrete population takes it much longer, skewed population requires
a larger sample if compared to the normal ones, and the Cauchy population
does not meet the condition of finite variance as required for ordinary CLT.
Therefore, `n = 30` can be treated as an informal rule and not valid universal
theorem.

## Limitations

The phrase “approximately normal” requires interpretation, and different
reasonable criteria may lead to slightly different cutoff values. In addition,
the exact results of the simulations depend on the reproducible random seed used
in them.
